blocks.text: Fourth, in this whole Psalm, as often elsewhere in the poetic books of the Hebrews, the two hemistichs are generally parallel and explain each other. From this it follows that יסע [col. 102] [II, 663] here is roughly the same as וינהג, and he brought in, in the second hemistich, in which we read that God by his power brought in the south wind. Fifth, if the matter is decided by authority, against the Greeks and Jerome we set the Chaldee and the Syriac, and both Arabic versions ^{(4)}, and the Hebrews, as many as there are, and the more recent interpreters, as many as I have been able to see. For not one of them occurs for whom יסע here means to take away. Rather, all understand that the east wind was stirred up and sent in by God. Pagninus: He stirred up the east wind in the heaven; Arias: He made the east wind set out in the heavens; Felix Pratensis: He moved the east wind in the heavens; Castalio: The east wind having been driven through the heaven. Add to these all the vernacular versions. Let this therefore stand: that God, according to David's meaning, moved this wind, not removed it; brought it in, not took it away. But for the matter to be understood, it must be noted that the Israelites were then in the desert of Paran, having already advanced a three days' journey beyond Mount Sinai, Num. X, 12. 33., and had the farthest gulf of the Arabian sea to the south; and therefore the wind that carried the quails from the Red Sea to their camp is rightly called by David תימן Theman, that is, southern. But why is the same wind called קדים kadim, that is, eastern? Aben Ezra and Kimchi answer that it is called by both names because it was מזרחי דרומי, that is, partly eastern, partly southern, which you might call in one word Euro-Notus ^{(5)}. This is utterly false. For that wind was in no way eastern, as those acquainted with the region know. Yet it is called קדים Kadim, and I shall now say why. Although four cardinal winds are established, which are in turn subdivided into many more, nevertheless the learned ^{b)} observe that in the ancient books of the philosophers and physicians, and especially in Aristotle and Theophrastus, to designate the conditions of weather and air produced by the winds, only τὰ βόρεια [ta boreia] and τὰ νότια [ta notia] are named, never τὰ ἑσπέρια [ta hesperia] or τὰ ἑῷα [ta heōa]. Hence Aristotle, Meteorol. book 2, ch. 6, after naming eight principal winds with their side-winds, says: Ὅλως δὲ τὰ μὲν βόρεια τούτων καλεῖται, τὰ δὲ νότια [Holōs de ta men boreia toutōn kaleitai, ta de notia]. In general, of these some are called northern, others southern. That is, the western winds, as colder, are assigned to the north wind, and the eastern ones to the south wind, because they are warmer. He adds this in these words: Προστίθηται δὲ τὰ μὲν ζεφυρικὰ τῷ βορέᾳ, ψυχρότερα γὰρ, διὰ τὸ ἀπὸ δυσμῶν πνεῖν· τῷ δὲ νότῳ ἀπηλιωτικὰ, θερμότερα γὰρ, τῷ (read διὰ τὸ) ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς πνεῖν [Prostithētai de ta men zephyrika tō borea, psychrotera gar, dia to apo dysmōn pnein; tō de notō apēliōtika, thermotera gar, tō (dia to) apo anatolēs pnein]. The eastern wind is warmer than the western for this reason, ὅτι πλείω χρόνον ὑπὸ τὸν ἥλιόν ἐστι [hoti pleiō chronon hypo ton hēlion esti], because it is longer under the sun. That is why [II, 664] in Greek it is called ἀπηλιώτης [apēliōtēs], and in Latin Subsolanus. Accordingly, in the Politics, book 4, ch. 3, the same Aristotle contends that all forms of commonwealth are to be referred either to democracy or to oligarchy, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν πνευμάτων λέγεται τὰ μὲν βόρεια, τὰ δὲ νότια, τάδ' ἄλλα τούτων παρεκβάσεις [kathaper epi tōn pneumatōn legetai ta men boreia, ta de notia, tad' alla toutōn parekbaseis], just as among the winds some are called northern, others southern, and the rest are deviations from these. Hence it is, he says, that they say τὸν μὲν ζέφυρον τοῦ βορέου, τοῦ δὲ νότου τὸν εὖρον [ton men zephyron tou boreou, tou de notou ton euron], that the zephyr belongs to the north wind, and the east wind to the south wind. To this belong the verses of Lucilius in the book on Cotys, king of the Thracians, which, badly corrupted in Nonius under the word Demagis, Salmasius restores thus:
King Cotys used to say that he knew only two winds, the south wind and the north wind, and moreover, that those little south winds from the storm-cloud he neither knew nor thought existed.
